# The problem

In label-free data a protein is often not observed in any sample of one group. Most of the time it is there, but below the limit of detection (LOD): the absence is information, not an unknown value. A linear model per protein cannot estimate a group without observations, so `lm` drops exactly these contrasts, often the ones with the largest changes.

```{r simulate}
library(prolfqua)
library(ggplot2)
sim <- sim_lfq_data_protein_config(Nprot = 100, weight_missing = 0.5, seed = 1234)
lfq <- LFQData$new(sim$data, sim$config)
contrasts <- c(AvsC = "group_A - group_Ctrl", BvsC = "group_B - group_Ctrl")

fa_lm <- build_contrast_analysis(lfq, "~ group_", contrasts, method = "lm")
lost <- fa_lm$get_missing()
lost
```

The intensities of these proteins show the empty groups:

```{r lostIntensities}
lfq$data_long() |>
  dplyr::filter(protein_Id %in% lost$protein_Id) |>
  dplyr::select(protein_Id, sampleName, abundance) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = sampleName, values_from = abundance) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

# The limit of detection

`MissingHelpers` estimates the LOD from the data. Groups in which a protein is observed in only one sample, or in the fewest samples, are the closest the data comes to the detection limit; the LOD is the median (`prob = 0.5`) of their mean intensities.

```{r lod}
mh <- MissingHelpers$new(lfq$data_long(), lfq$get_config())
mh$get_lod()
```

# lm_impute

`lm_impute` fits `lm` to every protein. Proteins whose fit fails, or leaves a coefficient undefined, are refitted with their missing values set to the LOD; observed values below the LOD are raised to it, because they cannot be told apart from it. A constant imputed value has no variance, so the residual variance of the refit would be too small; `lm_impute` borrows it from the proteins that could be fitted. The column `estimate_type` tells which route each estimate took. Pass `lod` to `build_contrast_analysis()` to use a LOD of your own.

```{r lmImpute}
fa_imp <- build_contrast_analysis(lfq, "~ group_", contrasts, method = "lm_impute")
res <- fa_imp$get_contrasts()
dplyr::count(res, contrast, estimate_type)
nrow(fa_imp$get_missing())
```

The estimates for the proteins that `lm` lost. A protein observed only near or below the LOD ends up with `diff` close to 0: there is no evidence that it changes.

```{r rescued}
res |>
  dplyr::semi_join(lost, by = c("protein_Id", "contrast")) |>
  dplyr::select(protein_Id, contrast, diff, p.value, FDR) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r volcano, fig.cap = "Volcano plot of lm_impute; colour marks the estimates refitted at the LOD."}
ggplot(res, aes(diff, -log10(p.value), colour = estimate_type)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~contrast) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Other methods

The same refit at the LOD is available with `limma_impute`, `limma_voom_impute` and `rfit_impute`. `hurdle_nested` takes a different route: it models the intensities and the peptide detection separately and combines their p-values. The number of estimated protein and contrast pairs per method:

```{r otherMethods}
methods <- c("lm", "lm_impute", "limma", "limma_impute", "rfit", "rfit_impute")
estimated <- vapply(methods, function(m) {
  nrow(build_contrast_analysis(lfq, "~ group_", contrasts, method = m)$get_contrasts())
}, integer(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = methods, estimated = estimated), row.names = FALSE)
```

The article [Comparing modelling methods on one dataset](https://fgcz.github.io/prolfqua/articles/ComparingMethods.html) compares them on peptide-level data, including the hurdle model.

# Completing the data matrix

`impute_from_model()` fills every missing cell with the prediction of its protein model: `fitted` for proteins fitted on their observed values, `lod_refit` for proteins refitted at the LOD, `complete` for proteins without missing values. The filled matrix is useful for heatmaps or clustering. The filled values carry no noise, so do not use them for further tests.

```{r fill}
filled <- impute_from_model(fa_imp$model, lfq)
table(filled$summary$route)
```

## Heatmap before and after

We cluster the proteins once, on the imputed data, and draw both heatmaps with that row order, so each row shows the same protein before and after.

```{r heatmapOrder}
before <- lfq$data_wide(as.matrix = TRUE)
after <- filled$lfqdata$data_wide(as.matrix = TRUE)
row_order <- rownames(after$data)[hclust(dist(t(scale(t(after$data)))))$order]
```

```{r heatmapBefore, fig.cap = "Before imputation: missing cells are grey."}
ht_before <- plot_heatmap(
  before$data, before$annotation, lfq$factor_keys(), lfq$sample_name(),
  na_fraction = 1, row_order = row_order
)
ht_before
```

```{r heatmapAfter, fig.cap = "After imputation: every cell holds a value."}
ht_after <- plot_heatmap(
  after$data, after$annotation, lfq$factor_keys(), lfq$sample_name(),
  na_fraction = 1, row_order = row_order
)
ht_after
```

## PCA before and after

PCA needs complete data. Before imputation it can only use the proteins without missing values; after imputation it uses all proteins.

```{r pca, fig.cap = "PCA before (top) and after (bottom) imputation.", fig.height = 8}
n_complete <- sum(filled$summary$route == "complete")
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
  lfq$get_Plotter()$pca() +
    ggtitle(paste0("Before imputation: ", n_complete, " complete proteins")),
  filled$lfqdata$get_Plotter()$pca() +
    ggtitle(paste0("After imputation: ", nrow(filled$summary), " proteins")),
  ncol = 1
)
```

After imputation the groups separate more cleanly, in the heatmap and in the PCA. Part of that is circular: each filled value is the model's estimate for its group, so imputation adds the group structure of the model to the data.
